# Why straight lanes and monolithic rotors do not provide passive self-centering by momentum redirection alone {#sec-no-self-centering}

This is the missing structural argument in many simple orbital-ring pictures.

Consider a nominally straight lane or monolithic rotor segment with a small transverse deflection $y(x,t)$. For small slope, the centerline curvature is approximately

$$
\kappa \approx y_{xx}.
$$

The moving stream must then be forced to follow that curved path. The stream exerts on the guide a reaction load per unit length of the form

$$
q_\mathrm{stream} \approx -T_\mathrm{eq} y_{xx},
$$ {#eq-stream-reaction}

where $T_\mathrm{eq}=\lambda v^2$ or $T_\mathrm{eq}=\dot m v$, depending on whether one uses the continuous or fixed-flux picture.

Now consider a sinusoidal perturbation,

$$
y(x,t) = Y\sin(kx).
$$

Then

$$
y_{xx} = -k^2 y,
$$

so the stream reaction becomes

$$
q_\mathrm{stream} = +T_\mathrm{eq} k^2 y.
$$ {#eq-anti-restoring}

That has the **same sign as the displacement**. If the lane is displaced upward at some point, the stream pushes upward there as well. The moving mass therefore pushes further into an existing curvature perturbation rather than restoring the lane to straightness.

This is not yet a complete stability model. Real dynamics also involve beam stiffness, membrane stiffness, damping, actuator delay, boundary conditions, and control law. But it is enough to establish the key point: a straight high-speed lane does not passively self-center by momentum redirection alone. The moving stream pushes into every bend of its path, with an anti-restoring stiffness $T_\mathrm{eq}k^2$, unless the surrounding structure and controls provide compensating reaction.

This is the central result of the mechanics of pipes conveying fluid, with the stream's $\lambda v^2$ in the place of the fluid's momentum flux [@housner1952bending; @paidoussis2014fluid]. That literature also settles what kind of instability it is. A stream guided along its whole path, with no free end, exerts forces that are conservative, and the structure fails by buckling, a static divergence [@benjamin1961dynamicsI; @holmes1978pipes]. The nonconservative "follower force" that makes a hose flail belongs to a pipe with a free end [@gregory1966unstableI], and a ring has none. This paper therefore calls the term of @eq-anti-restoring the path-following term, and its coefficient the path-following stiffness. Both names mean a conservative, anti-restoring stiffness. @sec-prior-work sets out the other earlier work the paper builds on.

That observation cuts directly against naive pictures of a single giant monolithic rotor or a set of parallel straight rotors simply going around Earth. Such concepts may contain enough momentum to generate support in principle, but they do not automatically contain a good structural answer to perturbations.
